title: The system: an online shop's product page behind four caches
caption: Each tier answers what it can and passes the rest inward; a change event removes stale copies from every tier.

steps.text: The browser keeps JS, CSS and photos for a year (versioned file names), so a repeat visit only asks for the product data. The CDN serves photos from the image store and the product API for 60 s.
A CDN miss reaches the product service. The top few thousand products sit in each pod's own memory for 5 s: no network hop at all.
Not in local memory: one GET product:42 to the shared cache cluster, about 1 ms. Most reads end here.
A miss reads the row from a DB replica and SETs it with a TTL (10 min plus random jitter), so the next reader hits.
A merchant changes the price. The writer commits it to the catalog DB, and the commit appears as a change event read from the DB log.
The invalidator turns the event into three removals: DEL the cache key, purge the CDN URL and tell every pod to drop its local copy. The TTL is the safety net if one is missed.

scenarios.name: Flash sale
scenarios.summary: A promoted product gets a sudden spike: each tier absorbs most of what reaches it, so the DB sees a trickle.

steps.text: A push notification sends a crowd to one product page within a minute.
The CDN answers almost every request; only about one request per edge location per 60 s reaches the service.
Every pod keeps the product locally, so the one cache node that owns product:42 sees one read per pod every 5 s, not every request.
When the entry expires, one request per pod refills it while the others wait (request coalescing), so the DB gets a handful of reads.

scenarios.name: Cache node down
scenarios.summary: Losing a cache node turns its keys into misses at once; protect the DB first, then let the cache warm up.

steps.text: One node of the cache cluster dies; every key it owned is now a miss.
Those misses hit the DB together. Pods cap concurrent DB reads (a bulkhead) and serve slightly stale local copies instead of queueing.
The replica of the dead node is promoted, or its slots move to other nodes, and the misses refill the cache key by key.
Alert on hit rate and DB read load: the drop and the recovery curve show how close the DB came to its limit.

scenarios.name: Schema change
scenarios.summary: A deploy adds a field to the cached product: change the key version instead of flushing the cache.

steps.text: New pods read and write product:v2:42; old pods still use product:v1:42. Neither misreads the other's format.
v2 keys start empty, so the rollout runs gradually (10% of pods, then more) to keep the extra DB reads small.
The invalidator deletes both versions during the rollout; v1 keys simply age out by TTL afterwards.
